Paul Graham.name: Paul Graham
topics: Startup ideas, ambition, and early founder judgment
sources: Paul Graham On Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders
advice: Choose a problem that feels difficult enough to matter. The most consequential startup ideas often look intimidating before they look inevitable.
Examine the founder's motivation as seriously as the market story. Serious ambition needs persistence, curiosity, and willingness to work through uncertainty.
Use new technical capability as a prompt to look again at old constraints, rather than assuming the technology itself is the company.
warnings: Do not reject an idea only because it initially looks frighteningly hard; difficulty can be part of the opportunity.
Do not mistake ambition for a large market-size story without a credible path through the hard parts.
questions: What makes this problem hard enough that others have avoided solving it?
Why will this founding team continue pursuing it when progress becomes slow or uncertain?

Michael Seibel.name: Michael Seibel
topics: Startup idea testing and early product execution
sources: How to Get and Test Startup Ideas
How To Build Product As A Small Startup
advice: Begin with a problem, preferably one you understand personally or are unusually well placed to solve.
After finding a promising problem, build a minimum viable product and put it in front of initial users quickly.
Use early conversations and early use to test whether the problem is real before investing heavily in features.
Use a repeatable product-release rhythm rather than treating product work as an endless feature list.
Give one person clear product ownership and connect each product cycle to a measurable outcome.
Turn ideas, bugs, and experiments into an explicit backlog; estimate effort, choose deliberately, assign work, test, and ship.
Tackle consequential difficult work rather than filling the roadmap with only easy tasks.
warnings: A polished idea without a clear problem or an initial-user path is weak evidence of demand.
Do not wait for perfect certainty before testing; the first useful evidence comes from real users.
Feature accumulation without a KPI or product theme creates activity without learning.
A small team can lose momentum when nobody owns the product decision process.
questions: Why are you qualified to work on this problem?
Who will use the first version, and how will you reach them?
Which measurable customer or business outcome should this product cycle improve?
What hard work are we avoiding, and is it the work that matters most?

Dalton Caldwell.name: Dalton Caldwell
sources: How to Apply and Succeed at Y Combinator
advice: Explain what you are building plainly. Clear communication signals clear thinking and makes it easier for others to understand the opportunity.
Tell a coherent founder-and-problem story: what happened, what you learned, what you are building, and why your team is suited to do it.
Do not assume that lacking a famous network prevents progress; make the work and evidence understandable on their own merits.
warnings: Avoid vague language, jargon, and claims that conceal the actual product, customer, or progress.
Do not treat fundraising or an application as a substitute for building evidence with users.
questions: Can a stranger understand the product, customer, and traction in a few sentences?
Does the story show evidence, or only aspiration?

Geoff Ralston.name: Geoff Ralston
topics: Founder persistence and customer-focused startup building
advice: Keep the work centered on making something people want; it is the discipline that should survive changing plans and startup pressure.
Treat startup progress as a continuing practice: keep learning from customers, keep improving the product, and keep moving forward after a program or milestone ends.
Use founder communities for momentum and feedback, but maintain responsibility for the actual customer problem.
warnings: A completed course, accelerator, pitch, or launch is not proof that the company has found product-market fit.
Do not let external validation replace persistent contact with the people the product is meant to serve.
questions: What evidence says that people want this now?
What will you do next week that gets the product closer to users?
